summary: This informational RFC describes IBAKE, an identity-based authenticated key exchange. Identity-based encryption simplifies infrastructure compared with certificates, but needs a private-key generator, which has its own limits. IBAKE addresses these by letting parties establish a key exchange with it.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people want a shared secret and use their names to make it. A trusted helper hands out special keys, and this explains how to get a secret together from them.

questions: how does ibake prevent key escrow
subtitle: Identity-based key exchange that avoids key escrow and provides mutual authentication.

tldr.problem: Identity-Based Encryption simplifies infrastructure compared to certificates, but a Private-Key Generator (PKG) can decrypt all communication (key escrow), and parties cannot mutually authenticate each other.
tldr.mechanism: IBAKE uses a three-message exchange where both parties encrypt with the other's identity-based public key. By including random Diffie-Hellman values (xP and yP) in the encrypted messages, they establish a shared session key xyP that only they can compute, preventing key escrow while proving identity.
tldr.outcome: Two parties can securely exchange keys and authenticate each other without certificates or high-availability PKG infrastructure, while perfect forward secrecy ensures session keys are always fresh and independent.

facts.label: Recommended curves
facts.value: NIST curves for ECDH, supersingular curves for IBE

today: RFC 6539 is an Informational specification published as an independent submission in March 2012. It has not been obsoleted and remains available for reference implementations of identity-based authenticated key exchange.

sections.title: The Problem with Certificates and IBE
sections.content:
Authenticated key agreement protocols let two or more participants authenticate each other and agree on encryption keys. Traditional public-key methods require Public Key Infrastructure (PKI): certificates, certificate authorities, and mechanisms for revocation. These have proved challenging to deploy and manage at scale.

Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) offers a simpler alternative: instead of certificates, participants use a trusted Private-Key Generator (PKG) that issues secret keys based on identities (such as email addresses or phone numbers). However, IBE has two significant limitations. First, the PKG becomes a key escrow entity: it can decrypt all communication because it issued all the secret keys. Second, traditional IBE does not provide mutual authentication between peers.

IBAKE (Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange) addresses both limitations. It allows two parties to establish a key that the PKG cannot compute, and it provides mutual authentication without certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular encryption needs fancy certificates, which are annoying. Identity-based encryption uses names instead, which is simpler, but the person who hands out keys can read everything. IBAKE fixes that: two people can make a secret even the key person cannot read.

sections.title: How IBAKE Works
sections.content:
IBAKE is a three-message exchange between an Initiator and a Responder. Both parties trust a PKG (which may be the same PKG or different PKGs for each party). They know each other's public identities and the PKG's public parameters, but do not share credentials beforehand.

In MESSAGE_1, the Initiator chooses a random x, computes xP (where P is a base point on an elliptic curve), and encrypts xP, its own identity (IDi), and the Responder's identity (IDr) using the Responder's identity-based public key. The Responder receives this, decrypts it using its secret key, learns xP, then chooses a random y and computes yP. It encrypts IDi, IDr, xP, and yP using the Initiator's public key to send in MESSAGE_2. The Initiator receives MESSAGE_2, decrypts it, verifies that the xP inside matches what it sent, and obtains yP. In MESSAGE_3, it encrypts IDi, IDr, and yP using the Responder's public key. Both parties can now compute xyP as the shared session key.
sections.plainLanguage: The Initiator sends a locked box containing a random number to the Responder. The Responder unlocks it, puts the number back inside, adds its own random number, and locks the box with the Initiator's key. The Initiator unlocks it, checks that both random numbers are right, and sends back the Responder's number in a locked box. Now both know a secret number that only they can compute.

sections.title: Why IBAKE Defeats Key Escrow
sections.content:
The key escrow problem is solved through the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) hardness assumption. All three messages are encrypted using IBE, so the PKG can decrypt them. However, even though the PKG observes xP and yP, it cannot compute xyP (the shared session key) from these values. Computing xyP from xP and yP is the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman problem, which is believed to be computationally hard.

Mutual authentication works because of message encryption and identity inclusion. Only the Responder (and its PKG) can decrypt MESSAGE_1, so it is the only non-PKG entity that learns xP. Similarly, only the Initiator (and its PKG) can decrypt MESSAGE_2. The Initiator verifies that xP reappears in MESSAGE_2, proving the message came from someone who decrypted MESSAGE_1 (i.e., the Responder). Similarly, the Responder verifies yP in MESSAGE_3, proving the message came from someone who decrypted MESSAGE_2. Assuming well-behaved PKGs, this establishes mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The PKG can read the locked boxes, but math says it cannot figure out the secret number from the two random numbers it sees. And because each message uses the right person's key and includes the other person's secret number, both parties know they are talking to the real person.

sections.title: Security Properties and Cryptographic Foundations
sections.content:
IBAKE provides several important security properties. Perfect forward and backward secrecy results from the random values x and y: even if one session key is compromised, past and future session keys remain secure because x and y are fresh for each exchange. No offline passwords are required: the protocol works for any two parties communicating for the first time, needing only knowledge of each other's public identities and PKG parameters.

The protocol relies on elliptic curves for both IBE operations and ECDH values. The specification recommends using a non-supersingular curve (such as NIST P-256) for ECDH point calculations (xP and yP), and a supersingular curve for IBE encryption and decryption. IBAKE reduces PKG availability requirements since the PKG need not be contacted during protocol execution, only when initially issuing keys. Time-bound identities (for example, by concatenating a date with the user identity) enable automatic key expiration, eliminating the need for real-time revocation mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone steals one secret message, old and new messages are still safe because each one uses fresh random numbers. You do not need to remember passwords, and the key server does not need to be online while you are talking. Keys can automatically expire when the date changes.

messages.label: MESSAGE_1: E(K_PUB_r, IDi || IDr || xP)
messages.note: Initiator sends its random point xP encrypted with Responder's public key.

messages.label: MESSAGE_2: E(K_PUB_i, IDi || IDr || xP || yP)
messages.note: Responder sends back xP and its random point yP encrypted with Initiator's public key.

messages.label: MESSAGE_3: E(K_PUB_r, IDi || IDr || yP)
messages.note: Initiator confirms receipt by sending back yP encrypted with Responder's public key.
